title: What Caused the Late Bronze Age Collapse?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Late Bronze Age collapse (around 1200 to 1150 BC, traditionally dated 1167 BC). They cover the Bronze Age itself (copper and tin trade, advances in farming, writing, government, and division of labor), the major civilizations of the period (Egyptians, Hittites, Canaanites, Cypriots, Minoans, Mycenaeans, Assyrians, Babylonians, and Sumerians as the starting point), and the competing theories for the collapse: the Sea Peoples as raiders, overextension, drought, earthquakes, a cascade of multiple disasters, and iron democratizing metalworking. They then discuss lessons for today (globalization and interdependence, economist Zachary Jones's view versus Eric Klein's view that modern systems are more fragile, resilience, climate change) and the Phoenicians rising afterward through purple dye trade. The episode ends with a listener mail about a crossword puzzle symmetry mix-up (radial versus mirror symmetry, and rebus squares).

entities.name: Eleven Sixty-Seven: The Year Civilization Collapsed

segments.title: Opening banter and Hulu plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with a tangent about the Hulu sketch show History of the World Part II, then introduce the Bronze Age as a period between the Stone Age and the Iron Age.
topics: History of the World Part II

segments.title: Bronze, trade networks, and early civilization
segments.summary: They explain how bronze is made from copper and tin, and how tin had to come from far away (Afghanistan), which required extensive trade networks. The hosts argue that these networks, plus better farming, division of labor, and centralized government, laid the foundations of civilization.

segments.title: Power, hierarchy, and the Bronze Age golden age
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the rise of hierarchical government and enslavement alongside cooperation and diplomacy, and describe a prosperous middle period of the Bronze Age.

segments.title: The Big Eight civilizations and the invention of writing
segments.summary: They list the major Bronze Age societies (Egyptians, Hittites, Canaanites, Cypriots, Minoans, Mycenaeans, Assyrians, Babylonians) and note that the Sumerians started it all with irrigation and writing. Writing allowed cross-checking between cultures and helped decipherment of scripts like Linear B.

segments.title: Collapse begins: timeline and the Iron Age
segments.summary: The collapse is dated to 1167 BC but unfolded over about thirty to forty years, around 1200 to 1150 BC. Cities were left in ruins, writing and languages were lost, and a Dark Age followed, with Iron Age successors like Sparta and Athens later.

segments.title: Sea Peoples, naming problems, and the Canaanites and Philistines
segments.summary: The Sea Peoples are introduced as a theory of raiders, a term coined by a French Egyptologist. The hosts note that contemporary names were lost, that Minoans and Sumerians were named later, and that the Philistines were long blamed for toppling the Canaanites but more recent scholarship suggests the Canaanites reformed as the Philistines after the collapse.

segments.title: Causes: overextension, drought, earthquakes, and iron
segments.summary: Theories covered include overextension of governments, a long drought (one hundred fifty years, possibly up to three hundred, with fossilized pollen from the Sea of Galilee), and earthquakes in a region where four plates meet. Evidence includes Hittite letters requesting grain from Egypt and buildings damaged by earthquakes and by attackers. The hosts favor a cascade of multiple disasters, and mention the idea that iron democratized metalworking and destabilized Bronze Age political order, as in Bronze Age Ireland. They also mention a theory that a planetoid impact brought metals near the surface.

segments.title: Lessons for today: globalization, interdependence, and resilience
segments.summary: The hosts discuss lessons: over-globalization and interdependence can spread failures. They cite economist Zachary Jones, who argues modern wealth provides a cushion, and Eric Klein, professor of ancient Near Eastern studies and author of Eleven Sixty-Seven, who argues modern systems may be more fragile. They conclude resilience is the best response, and discuss secession and climate change as related issues.

segments.title: Phoenicians and purple dye
segments.summary: After the collapse, the Phoenicians rose as a seafaring people and spread purple dye across the Mediterranean, establishing new trade networks that restarted prosperity.

segments.title: Listener mail: crossword symmetry and rebus
segments.summary: Listeners Alec and David write in to correct Chuck's claim about crossword symmetry; the hosts were describing radial (rotational) symmetry, not mirror symmetry. Josh explains rebus squares, which put multiple letters in one square, and the hosts sign off with a joke about string theory.
